partner_context.their_ambition: San Francisco Bay Ferry is the public transit ferry service on San Francisco Bay, run by WETA — the San Francisco Bay Area Water Emergency Transportation Authority, a California state agency created in 2007. It carried about 3.0 million riders in 2025 across 6 routes and 9 terminals, and doubles as the region's water-based emergency network when bridges and roads are out.
partner_context.their_pressure: WETA's Rapid Electric Emission Free (REEF) program is bringing battery-electric ferries into service from 2027, and the Sea Change — the first commercial hydrogen fuel-cell ferry in the United States — has already operated on the Bay. Growth and the net-zero mandate both demand fleet renewal without disturbing the services people rely on today.
partner_context.where_navier_fits: Navier is the zero-emission, software-defined passenger-only foiling layer above the Bay Ferry network — fast, frequent, low-wake hops on the busy commute crossings (the Ferry Building to Oakland, Alameda, Richmond and Vallejo) that complement WETA's electrification, plus quiet access to the new and committed landings the big boats can't serve economically.

differentiation.why_navier: Software-defined and autonomy-ready — the same DNA as the autonomous road programs — built for fleet operation, with a ~100-vessel network proving the model in the Maldives.

proof_points.claim: The authority runs marine transport at public scale.
proof_points.evidence: Routes incl. Ferry Building – Oakland/Alameda, Ferry Building – Vallejo/Mare Island, Ferry Building – Richmond, Ferry Building – Harbor Bay, Ferry Building – Alameda Seaplane, and Oakland – South San Francisco; committed expansion to Mission Bay, Treasure Island, Berkeley and Redwood City.
proof_points.source: San Francisco Bay Area Water Emergency Transportation Authority (WETA), trading as San Francisco Bay Ferry

proof_points.claim: There is a published growth and decarbonization mandate.
proof_points.evidence: WETA's Rapid Electric Emission Free (REEF) program is bringing battery-electric ferries into service from 2027, and the Sea Change — the first commercial hydrogen fuel-cell ferry in the United States — has already operated on the Bay.
proof_points.source: WETA Strategic & Short Range Transit Plans; Rapid Electric Emission Free (REEF) program; California clean-transportation goals

proof_points.evidence: Hydrofoiling, software-governed vessels — the same DNA arriving in autonomous road mobility — built for fleet operation.

proof_points.claim: The fleet model is real and at scale.
proof_points.evidence: ~100 vessels / $100M / 3-year phasing proving the network model in the Maldives; 10 vessels delivered, 4,000+ flight hours; a demo vessel is on the water now.

objections.concern: Does this compete with the existing public ferry service?
objections.response: No — Navier is a passenger-only foiling layer above the existing service, adding fast frequencies on the busy corridors the conventional boats can't run economically. It complements the electrification already underway.
Pioneer II needs only a berth pedestal at existing piers — no new shore power, vertiports or rights-of-way.

objections.concern: Is foiling safe in busy, shared public waterways?
objections.response: Foiling is software-governed — geofenced no-foil and low-wake zones near piers, ferry lanes and moorings, automatic speed and wake limits in shared water, and conventional low-speed handling everywhere it isn't cleared to fly.

the_ask.navier_brings: The software-defined foiling fleet (Pioneer II + long-range hybrid), the Maldives-proven network playbook, certification and operations.
the_ask.partner_brings: Network integration, berth access, the published network mandate and regulatory cover.
the_ask.next_step: A pilot on the busiest corridors, co-specified with the authority against its published network and net-zero targets.

close.title: A zero-emission water layer that grows with the city.
close.body: Start on the busiest corridors, scale across the full network, then mature the service — a zero-emission foiling tier that advances the authority's net-zero mandate while the services people rely on keep running underneath.

why_navier_now.step_change: Hydrofoiling lifts the hull clear of the water, so a Navier vessel flies instead of plowing through chop — roughly 10x more efficient than a conventional planing boat, faster (30+ kt cruise), and dramatically smoother and quieter. It's software-defined and autonomy-ready, so the same fleet keeps getting better and cheaper to run over time.
why_navier_now.no_new_infrastructure: Navier rides on infrastructure that already exists — the open water and the piers already in use. No vertiports, no new rights-of-way, no tunnels or tracks. Pioneer II needs only a berth pedestal; the long-range hybrid needs no charging infrastructure at all.
why_navier_now.the_moment: Three forces just converged: the technology crossed from prototype to platform (10 vessels delivered, 4,000+ flight hours, 2025 production sold out), decarbonization mandates turned legacy diesel fleets into stranded liabilities, and the hybrid removed the charging excuse. The marine layer is being claimed cluster-by-cluster right now.

public_value.headline: What it returns to the public
public_value.note: The authority's real bottom line. Quantified outputs (emissions avoided, congestion relieved, time saved, access widened) are produced with the authority under the PTA economics convention.
levers: Emissions avoided — zero-emission foiling alongside WETA's own REEF battery-electric program and the Sea Change hydrogen demonstrator
Congestion relieved — passenger trips shifted off the Bay Bridge, I-80 and I-880 onto fast water
Time saved — fast passenger-only crossings on the commute corridors the conventional ferries run more slowly
Access widened — frequent service to the committed Mission Bay, Treasure Island, Berkeley and Redwood City landings
Resilience — a zero-emission fast-ferry layer that reinforces WETA's water-emergency mandate when bridges and roads are out
